Paper Title: AART: AI-Assisted Red-Teaming with Diverse Data Generation for New LLM-powered Applications
Description: The AART dataset contains 3,269 English prompts and was created through AI assisted red teaming to support automated adversarial testing of large language models. It targets safety domains including physical and public safety, discrimination and hate, toxicity, and information integrity. Entries were generated using an AI driven pipeline designed to produce diverse and application relevant adversarial test cases.

Paper Title:
Why Should Adversarial Perturbations be Imperceptible?
Rethink the Research Paradigm in Adversarial NLP
Description: The AdvBench dataset contains 1,000 single turn English prompts focused on physical and public safety harms, including violence and criminal activity. It was created to support research on security oriented adversarial NLP by providing a benchmark that reflects real world attacker goals. Entries were designed for generation based adversarial evaluation.

Paper Title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned
Description: The Anthropic RedTeam dataset contains 38,961 multi-turn English dialogue examples covering safety domains such as physical and public safety, discrimination and toxicity, and sexual content. It was created as part of Anthropic’s red teaming efforts to surface harmful model behaviors and includes human-generated adversarial conversations used in harmlessness training and evaluation.

Paper Title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
Description: The Anthropic HarmlessBase dataset contains 44,849 multi-turn English dialogues annotated for safety across domains including physical and public safety, discrimination and toxicity, and sexual content. It consists of red teaming style prompts and responses used to build and evaluate harmlessness models, forming a core component of the HH-RLHF training data.

Paper Title: Bot-Adversarial Dialogue for Safe Conversational Agents
Description: [Bot-Adversarial Dialogue] is a dataset by Facebook AI Research featuring 5,000 adversarial dialogues where humans intentionally provoke chatbots into generating toxic outputs. It contains over 79,000 utterances designed to train safety classifiers that detect context-dependent offenses rather than just static hate speech.

Paper Title: BBQ: A hand-built bias benchmark for question answering
Description: The BBQ dataset contains 58,492 English examples designed to evaluate how strongly language models rely on social stereotypes in question answering. It targets discrimination and bias by presenting under-informative and fully informative contexts to test whether models default to biased assumptions or override biases when the correct answer is clear.

Paper Title: BeaverTails: Towards Improved Safety Alignment of LLM via a Human-Preference Dataset
Description: The BeaverTails dataset contains 333,963 English examples covering physical and public safety risks, discrimination and toxicity, and deceptive content. It was created to support safety alignment research and includes a large classification dataset, a preference dataset, and an evaluation set of GPT and human-written prompts. It is widely used for training and assessing LLM safety behaviors.

Paper Title: Towards Identifying Social Bias in Dialog Systems: Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark
Description: The CDial-Bias dataset contains 28,343 Chinese dialogue examples focused on social bias and toxicity in conversational settings. It was created to measure biased or harmful language in dialogue systems and includes detailed annotations for context sensitivity, targeted groups, and fine-grained bias categories.

Paper Title: Safety-Tuned LLaMAs: Lessons From Improving the Safety of Large Language Models that Follow Instructions
Can LLMs Keep a Secret? Testing Privacy Implications of Language Models via Contextual Integrity Theory
Description: The ConfAIde dataset contains 1,326 English examples focused on legal and compliance risks. It was created to evaluate how well language models avoid generating content that violates legal standards or compliance requirements.

Paper Title: Purple Llama CyberSecEval: A Secure Coding Benchmark for Language Models
Description: The Cyberattack Assistance dataset contains 1,000 English examples targeting physical and public safety risks in the cybersecurity domain. It was created as part of Meta’s Purple Llama initiative to test whether language models provide or refuse harmful cyberattack assistance.

Paper Title: DecodingTrust: A Comprehensive Assessment of Trustworthiness in GPT Models
Description: The DecodingTrust dataset includes 243,877 English examples from the safety-related sections of the benchmark. It was created to assess trustworthiness in GPT models across areas such as misinformation, factuality, toxicity, bias, robustness, privacy, and machine ethics.

Paper Title: SORRY-Bench: Systematically Evaluating Large Language Model Safety Refusal
Description: SORRY-Bench is a safety refusal benchmark containing 450 class-balanced unsafe instructions across 45 risk categories which are augmented with 20 linguistic mutations to generate 9,000 adversarial prompts. It utilizes a fine-tuned LLM judge to systematically evaluate how models handle diverse refusal triggers and stylized malicious requests beyond standard safety compliance.

Paper Title: Lakera’s Prompt Injection Test (PINT)—A New Benchmark for Evaluating Prompt Injection Solutions
Description: Lakera PINT is a comprehensive safety benchmark containing over 3,000 adversarial inputs that evaluate prompt injection detection systems against direct attacks, jailbreaks, and hard-negative false positives. This dataset remains closed-source to ensure evaluation integrity and prevent training contamination while providing a standardized open-source framework for measuring defense robustness against evolving injection techniques.

Paper Title: Many-Turn Jailbreaking
Description: MTJ-Bench is a safety benchmark designed to evaluate the fragility of LLM defenses in multi-turn conversations. Unlike single-shot attacks, it measures "jailbreak persistence" testing whether a model, once tricked into an initial harmful response, remains compromised when fielding subsequent relevant or irrelevant follow-up questions (the "Free Lunch" effect).

Paper Title: Jailbreak Distillation: Renewable Safety Benchmarking
Description: JBDistill-Bench is a renewable safety benchmark framework that systematically "distills" dynamic jailbreak attacks into high-quality static datasets. It utilizes a small set of development models to filter and select the most effective adversarial prompts which allows for fair and reproducible safety evaluations without the high computational costs of running live attacks for every new model.

Paper Title: JBShield: Defending Large Language Models from Jailbreak Attacks through Activated Concept Analysis and Manipulation
Description: JBShield is a defense framework and evaluation dataset that detects jailbreaks by analyzing "activated concepts" within an LLM's hidden representations to distinguish between malicious and benign intent. It utilizes the Linear Representation Hypothesis to identify and suppress toxic subspaces across nine distinct attack types and five target models which reduces attack success rates from 61% to 2%.

Paper Title: SoK: Taxonomy and Evaluation of Prompt Security in Large Language Models
Description: JailbreakDB is the largest annotated prompt security dataset to date, containing over 1.5 million examples (445k jailbreaks and 1M benign prompts) aggregated from 14 diverse sources. It serves as a unified foundation for training safety classifiers and benchmarking defenses by providing standardized, lightweight labels for attack tactics, sources, and jailbreak status across a massive scale.

Paper Title: JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
Description: JailbreakBench is an open-source, standardized benchmark for LLM safety that combines an evolving repository of successful adversarial prompts, called jailbreak artifacts, with a reproducible evaluation framework and leaderboard. It includes the core JBB-Behaviors dataset, featuring 100 distinct harmful misuse behaviors and 100 benign behaviors to track progress in both attack generation and defense mechanisms.

Paper Title: GuidedBench: Measuring and Mitigating the Evaluation Discrepancies of In-the-wild LLM Jailbreak Methods
Description: GuidedBench is a novel safety benchmark that shifts from generalized scoring to a nuanced, case-by-case evaluation paradigm for jailbreak attacks, comprising a curated harmful question dataset and integrated detailed scoring guidelines (GuidedEval). It addresses misleading effectiveness scores in previous benchmarks, demonstrating a 76.03% reduction in inter-evaluator variance for more reliable and reproducible safety assessments.

Paper Title: GuardSet-X: Massive Multi-Domain Safety Policy-Grounded Guardrail Dataset
Description: GuardSet-X is the first large-scale, multi-domain, policy-grounded guardrail dataset, offering 100,000+ data instances grounded in 150+ official safety policies across eight safety-critical domains (e.g., finance, law, code generation). It establishes a principled, comprehensive benchmark for LLM guardrails, providing a fine-grained hierarchy of 400+ risk categories to rigorously evaluate model compliance and domain-specific specialization.

Paper Title: ClearHarm: A more challenging jailbreak dataset
Description: ClearHarm is a challenging jailbreak benchmark focused on testing LLMs against unambiguously harmful, single-use questions, specifically those concerning CBRN (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear) threats and malicious code. This dataset consists of 179 carefully curated prompts designed to be intrinsically harmful, ensuring models should always refuse, regardless of context or phrasing, making it an ideal resource for evaluating catastrophic misuse risk.

Paper Title: DICES Dataset: Diversity in Conversational AI Evaluation for Safety
Description: The DICES350 dataset contains 350 English items designed to evaluate discrimination and bias through rater diversity and meta evaluation. It was created to study how different annotator backgrounds influence bias assessments in language model outputs.

Paper Title: Do-Not-Answer: A Dataset for Evaluating Safeguards in LLMs
Description: The Do-Not-Answer dataset contains 939 English prompts covering unsafe topics such as criminal activity, sexual harm, child harm, hate, and toxicity. It was created to test whether language models appropriately refuse dangerous or harmful queries.

Paper Title: "Do Anything Now": Characterizing and Evaluating In-The-Wild Jailbreak Prompts on Large Language Models
Description: The DAN dataset contains 6,387 English jailbreak prompts, with an expanded version of 46,800 items. It targets safety risks related to crime, violence, hate, toxicity, and sexual content, and was created to evaluate model vulnerability to “do anything now” style jailbreak attacks.

Paper Title: Gandalf the Red: Adaptive Security for LLMs
Description: The Gandalf dataset contains 1,000 English prompts designed to test deception and prompt injection risks. It evaluates whether a model can be manipulated into ignoring instructions or leaking protected information.

Paper Title: Ignore This Title and HackAPrompt: Exposing Systemic Vulnerabilities of LLMs through a Global Scale Prompt Hacking Competition
Description: The HackAPrompt dataset contains 601,757 multilingual prompts, primarily in English, focused on deception and prompt injection attacks. It was created to benchmark how effectively models resist adversarial attempts to override system instructions.

Paper Title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
Description: The HarmBench text dataset contains 400 English prompts covering criminal and violent content, professional biosafety topics in biology and chemistry, and cybersecurity threats. It was created to evaluate model safety performance across multiple high risk domains.

Paper Title: HateXplain: A Benchmark Dataset for Explainable Hate Speech Detection
Description: HateXplain is the first benchmark hate speech dataset designed for explainable AI (XAI), moving beyond simple classification to address model bias and interpretability. Its unique value lies in token-level rationales that justify human annotation decisions, which can be used to train models to reduce unintended bias towards target communities.

Paper Title: StereoSet: Measuring stereotypical bias in pretrained language models
Description: StereoSet is a large-scale, natural English dataset designed to quantify and track stereotypical biases present in pretrained language models. It evaluates bias across four domains (gender, profession, race, and religion). The dataset uses the Context Association Test (CAT), involving both intrasentence and intersentence tasks, to measure both the model's language modeling ability and its stereotypical preference. The primary goal is to assess the model's tendency to rank stereotypical sentences higher than anti-stereotypical or unrelated sentences.

Paper Title: CrowS-Pairs: A Challenge Dataset for Measuring Social Biases in Masked Language Models
Description: CrowS-Pairs is a crowdsourced challenge dataset of 1,508 English sentence pairs designed to measure the degree of U.S. stereotypical biases present in Masked Language Models (MLMs). It covers nine bias types (including race, gender, and socioeconomic status), evaluating whether a model preferentially assigns higher pseudo-log-likelihood scores to the more stereotypical sentence in the pair.

Paper Title: BOLD: Dataset and Metrics for Measuring Biases in Open-Ended Language Generation
Description: BOLD is the largest fairness benchmark dataset to-date (at the time of publication) specifically for studying and benchmarking social biases in open-ended language generation. It consists of text generation prompts extracted from English Wikipedia sentences, designed to measure how Language Models (LMs) disproportionately generate negative, unfair, or stereotypical text against certain groups when prompted. It introduced new automated metrics, including toxicity, psycholinguistic norms, and text gender polarity, to measure bias from multiple angles.

Paper Title: RealToxicityPrompts: Evaluating Neural Toxic Degeneration in Language Models
Description: RealToxicityPrompts is a foundational safety benchmark dataset specifically designed to evaluate neural toxic degeneration in Large Language Models (LLMs). It consists of naturally occurring sentence prefixes (prompts) sourced from the OpenWebText Corpus, which are fed to an LLM to assess its tendency to complete the prompt with toxic language. The prompts are scored using the Perspective API to provide toxicity labels for the model's generated continuation.

Paper Title: ToxicChat: Unveiling Hidden Challenges of Toxicity Detection in Real-World User-AI Conversation
Description: ToxicChat is a novel safety benchmark based on real user prompts collected from the Vicuna online demo and Chatbot Arena, explicitly focusing on the unique challenges of toxicity detection in user-AI conversations. The dataset reveals a significant domain difference compared to social media-derived content, often containing nuanced and implicit toxic queries that existing moderation models struggle to identify. It is meticulously annotated using a human-AI collaborative framework to ensure high quality, with labels for both toxicity and jailbreaking attempts.

Paper Title: SafeInfer: Context Adaptive Decoding Time Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
Description: The HarmEval dataset contains 550 prompts, each representing an unsafe question or instruction. It is designed to assess how language models handle potential misuse scenarios. All entries are written in English and were machine-generated based on OpenAI and Meta usage policies. The dataset’s license has not been specified.

Paper Title: Measuring Implicit Bias in Explicitly Unbiased Large Language Models
Description: The ImplicitBias dataset includes 33,600 prompts, consisting of either Implicit Association Test (IAT) word-association tasks or decision-making scenarios. It was developed to measure implicit bias in large language models. All content is in English, created through a hybrid process that combines IAT-style templates with custom sociodemographic attributes and LLM-generated decision scenarios. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Paper Title: Fairness through Difference Awareness: Measuring Desired Group Discrimination in LLMs
Description: The DifferenceAwareness dataset contains 16,000 prompts, each formatted as a question. It was developed to assess how well large language models recognize and handle differences across groups. All entries are written in English and were created by humans, drawing partly from existing benchmarks and partly from newly authored questions. The dataset is distributed under the CC0 1.0 Universal license.

Paper Title: MedSafetyBench: Evaluating and Improving the Medical Safety of Large Language Models
Description: The MedSafetyBench dataset consists of 1,800 conversations, each featuring an unsafe medical request paired with a corresponding safe response. It was created to evaluate the medical safety performance of large language models. All entries are in English and were machine-generated using GPT-4 and Llama-2-7b. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Paper Title: The PRISM Alignment Dataset: What Participatory, Representative and Individualised Human Feedback Reveals About the Subjective and Multicultural Alignment of Large Language Models
Description: The PRISM dataset contains 8,011 conversations, which may span multiple turns and include user messages alongside responses from one or more language models. It was developed to capture the diversity of human preferences regarding LLM behavior. All content is in English and was written by crowdworkers. The dataset is provided under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license.

Paper Title: WildGuard: Open One-Stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs
Description: The WildGuardMix dataset includes 86,759 examples, each consisting of either a standalone prompt or a prompt–response pair annotated for safety. It was developed to support the training and evaluation of content-moderation guardrails. All entries are in English and were produced through a hybrid process: 87% synthetic data, 11% real user–LLM interactions, and 2% annotator-written content. The dataset is released under the ODC BY license.

Paper Title: SG-Bench: Evaluating LLM Safety Generalization Across Diverse Tasks and Prompt Types
Description: The SGBench dataset contains 1,442 prompts, each presenting a malicious question or instruction in various formats, including direct queries, jailbreak attempts, multiple-choice items, and safety-classification tasks. It was designed to assess how well LLM safety mechanisms generalize across different tasks and prompt styles. All entries are in English and originate from human-written sources, sampled from AdvBench, HarmfulQA, BeaverTails, and SaladBench, then expanded using templates and additional LLM-generated variations. The dataset is released under the GPL 3.0 license.

Paper Title: The Art of Saying No: Contextual Noncompliance in Language Models
Description: The CoCoNot dataset contains 12,478 prompts, each written as a question or instruction that models are expected not to follow. It was created to evaluate and strengthen contextual non compliance in large language models. All entries are in English and were produced through a hybrid process in which human written seed prompts were expanded using LLMs. The dataset is distributed under the MIT license.

Paper Title: Language Model Alignment in Multilingual Trolley Problems
Description: MultiTP comprises 107,000 binary-choice questions presenting trolley-style moral dilemmas to evaluate the cross-cultural stability of AI decision-making across 106 languages. Generated through a hybrid process of sampling from the Moral Machine experiment and templated translation, this massive benchmark tests whether Large Language Models maintain consistent ethical alignment regardless of the input language.

Paper Title: "Do Anything Now": Characterizing and Evaluating In-The-Wild Jailbreak Prompts on Large Language Models
Description: The ForbiddenQuestions dataset contains 390 prompts, each written as a question that targets behaviour prohibited by OpenAI. It was created to test whether large language models respond to questions that violate OpenAI usage policies. All entries are in English and were machine generated using GPT written templates that were expanded through combinatorial methods. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Paper Title: CoSafe: Evaluating Large Language Model Safety in Multi-Turn Dialogue Coreference
Description: The CoSafe dataset contains 1,400 conversations, each structured as a multi turn exchange in which the final user question is unsafe. It was created to evaluate how well large language models handle safety in dialogue settings that involve coreference. All content is in English and was produced through a hybrid process that began with sampling material from BeaverTails and continued with GPT 4 expansions into full multi turn conversations. The dataset does not specify a license.

Paper Title: Social Bias Probing: Fairness Benchmarking for Language Models
Description: The SoFa dataset contains 1,490,120 English sentences, each mentioning a single sociodemographic group. It was created to assess social biases in large language models. Entries were produced through a hybrid process that sampled templates from SBIC and combined them with various sociodemographic groups. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

The ArabicAdvBench dataset contains 520 prompts, each presenting a harmful instruction paired with a corresponding jailbreak prompt. It was created to assess safety risks in large language models operating in different forms of Arabic. All entries are machine generated, produced by translating the AdvBench dataset, which is itself synthetically created. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Language: Arabic, English, Filipino, French, Hindi, Russian, Serbian, Spanish
Paper Title: The Multilingual Alignment Prism: Aligning Global and Local Preferences to Reduce Harm
Description: The AyaRedTeaming dataset contains 7,419 prompts, each written as a harmful question or instruction. It was created to support research on alignment by providing a testbed that reflects both global and local safety preferences. The dataset includes content in Arabic, English, Filipino, French, Hindi, Russian, Serbian, and Spanish. All entries were written by paid native speaking annotators. The dataset is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Paper Title: Controllable Preference Optimization: Toward Controllable Multi-Objective Alignment
Description: The UltraSafety dataset contains 3,000 prompts, each consisting of a harmful instruction paired with a jailbreak prompt. It was created to provide data for safety fine tuning of large language models. All entries are in English and were machine generated by sampling from AdvBench and MaliciousInstruct and expanding the material using SelfInstruct. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Paper Title: Gender Bias in Decision-Making with Large Language Models: A Study of Relationship Conflicts
Description: The DeMET dataset includes 29 scenarios, each portraying a married couple with two name placeholders who must make a decision. It was designed to assess gender bias in the decision making of large language models. All scenarios are written in English and were created by the authors, drawing inspiration from a WHO questionnaire. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Language: Belarussian, Russian, Ukrainian, Croatian, Serbian, Slovene, Czech, Polish, Slovak, English
Paper Title: Women Are Beautiful, Men Are Leaders: Gender Stereotypes in Machine Translation and Language Modeling
Description: The GEST dataset contains 3,565 sentences, each reflecting a specific gender stereotype. It was created to evaluate gender stereotypical reasoning in language models and in machine translation systems. The dataset includes material in Belarussian, Russian, Ukrainian, Croatian, Serbian, Slovene, Czech, Polish, Slovak, and English. All sentences were written by professional translators and later validated by the authors. The dataset is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

The GenMO dataset contains 908 scenarios, each depicting a person in an everyday situation where their actions can be evaluated as moral or immoral. It was created to assess gender bias in the moral decision making of large language models. All content is in English and was drawn from human written material sampled from MoralStories, ETHICS, and SocialChemistry. The dataset does not specify a license.

The CIVICS dataset contains 699 excerpts, each consisting of a short passage that expresses or implies a social or cultural value. It was created to evaluate how large language models vary across languages and value sensitive topics. The dataset includes material in German, Italian, French, and English. All excerpts are human written and were sampled from government and media sources. The dataset is released under the CC BY 4.0 license.

Paper Title: Towards Measuring the Representation of Subjective Global Opinions in Language Models
Description: The GlobalOpinionQA dataset contains 2,556 multiple choice questions and was created to examine which groups’ opinions are most closely reflected in the responses of large language models. All questions are in English and were adapted from Pew’s Global Attitudes surveys and from the World Values Survey, both written by professional survey designers. The dataset is released under the CC BY NC SA 4.0 license.

Language: Arabic, Chinese, Czech, Dutch, English, French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swedish
Paper Title: Towards Measuring the Representation of Subjective Global Opinions in Language Models
Description: The PolygloToxicityPrompts dataset contains 425,000 prompts, each consisting of an unfinished document. It was created to evaluate how likely large language models are to produce toxic content across seventeen languages. The dataset includes material in Arabic, Chinese, Czech, Dutch, English, French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, and Swedish. All entries are human written and were sampled from mC4 and The Pile. The dataset is released under the AI2 ImpACT – LR license.

Paper Title: CALM : A Multi-task Benchmark for Comprehensive Assessment of Language Model Bias
Description: The CALM dataset contains 78,400 examples, each formatted as a question answering item, a sentiment classification task, or a natural language inference task. It was created to assess gender and racial bias in large language models across a range of domains and task types. All entries are in English and were produced through a hybrid process in which human designed templates were inspired by existing datasets and then expanded through combinatorial generation. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Paper Title: CHiSafetyBench: A Chinese Hierarchical Safety Benchmark for Large Language Models
Description: The CHiSafetyBench dataset contains 1,861 multiple choice questions and was created to assess how well large language models can recognize risky content and decline to answer unsafe questions in Chinese. All entries are in Chinese and were produced through a hybrid process that combined material sampled from SafetyBench and SafetyPrompts with additional prompts generated by GPT 3.5. The dataset does not specify a license.

Paper Title: Automatic Pseudo-Harmful Prompt Generation for Evaluating False Refusals in Large Language Models
Description: The PHTest dataset contains 3,260 prompts, each written as a pseudo harmful question or instruction. It was created to evaluate false refusals in large language models. All entries are in English and were machine generated using Llama2 7B Chat, Llama3 8B Instruct, and Mistral 7B Instruct V0.2. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Paper Title: SafetyBench: Evaluating the Safety of Large Language Models
Description: The SafetyBench dataset contains 11,435 multiple choice questions and was created to evaluate the safety performance of large language models through structured MCQ testing. The dataset includes material in both English and Chinese. Entries were produced through a hybrid process that drew on existing datasets and Chinese exam sources, followed by further augmentation using LLMs. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Paper Title: Language Models are Homer Simpson! Safety Re-Alignment of Fine-tuned Language Models through Task Arithmetic
Description: The CatQA dataset contains 550 prompts, each presented as a question. It was created to evaluate the effectiveness of safety training methods for large language models. The dataset includes material in English, Chinese, and Vietnamese. All entries were machine generated by an unnamed model that was not safety tuned. The dataset is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Paper Title: KorNAT: LLM Alignment Benchmark for Korean Social Values and Common Knowledge
Description: The KorNAT dataset contains 10,000 multiple choice questions, each describing a specific social scenario. It was created to assess how closely large language models align with South Korean social values. The dataset includes content in English and Korean. All entries were produced through a hybrid process in which GPT 3.5 generated questions based on keywords drawn from media sources and public surveys. The dataset is released under the CC BY NC 4.0 license.

Paper Title: CMoralEval: A Moral Evaluation Benchmark for Chinese Large Language Models
Description: The CMoralEval dataset contains 30,388 multiple choice questions, each centered on a specific moral scenario. It was created to evaluate the moral reasoning abilities of Chinese large language models. All content is in Chinese and was produced through a hybrid process that involved sampling material from Chinese television programs and other media, then converting these sources into question templates using GPT 3.5. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Language: English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali, Russian, Japanese, German
Paper Title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
Description: The XSafety dataset contains 28,000 prompts, each written as a question or instruction. It was created to evaluate the safety of multilingual large language models. The dataset includes material in English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali, Russian, Japanese, and German. Entries were produced through a hybrid process that sampled prompts from SafetyPrompts, then translated them automatically and validated the results. The dataset is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Paper Title: SALAD-Bench: A Hierarchical and Comprehensive Safety Benchmark for Large Language Models
Description: The SaladBench dataset contains 21,000 prompts, each written as a question or instruction. It was created to evaluate LLM safety as well as the effectiveness of attack and defense techniques. All content is in English and was produced through a hybrid process that drew heavily on existing datasets and then augmented the material using GPT 4. The dataset is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Language: English, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Vietnamese
Description: The MMHB dataset contains 5,754,444 prompts, each written as a sentence that begins a two person conversation. It was created to evaluate sociodemographic biases in large language models across multiple languages. The dataset includes material in English, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, and Vietnamese. Entries were produced through a hybrid process in which templates were sampled from HolisticBias, then translated and further expanded. The dataset does not specify a license.

Paper Title: GPTFUZZER: Red Teaming Large Language Models with Auto-Generated Jailbreak Prompts
Description: The GPTFuzzer dataset contains 100 prompts, each presented as a question or instruction. It was created to evaluate the effectiveness of an automated red teaming method for large language models. All entries are in English and were produced through a hybrid process that sampled material from AnthropicHarmlessBase along with an unpublished GPT generated dataset. The dataset is released under the MIT license.

Paper Title: ALERT: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Safety through Red Teaming
Description: The ALERT dataset contains 44,800 prompts, each written as a question or instruction. It was created to evaluate the safety of large language models using red teaming techniques. All entries are in English and were produced through a hybrid process that sampled material from AnthropicRedTeam and then expanded it using templates. The dataset is released under the CC BY NC SA 4.0 license.

Paper Title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
Description: The ORBench dataset contains 80,000 prompts, each written as a question or instruction. It was created to evaluate false refusal in large language models at scale. All entries are in English and were machine generated by first using Mixtral to produce toxic prompts, then rewriting them into safe versions, followed by filtering. The dataset is released under the CC BY 4.0 license.

Paper Title: S-Eval: Towards Automated and Comprehensive Safety Evaluation for Large Language Models
Description: The Flames dataset contains 2,251 prompts, each written as a question or instruction. It was created to assess the value alignment of Chinese language large language models. All content is in Chinese and was written by crowdworkers. The dataset is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Paper Title: S-Eval: Towards Automated and Comprehensive Safety Evaluation for Large Language Models
Description: The SEval dataset contains 20,000 prompts, each written as an unsafe question or instruction. It was created to evaluate the safety performance of large language models. The dataset includes content in English and Chinese. All entries were machine generated using a fine tuned Qwen 14B model. The dataset is released under the CC BY NC SA 4.0 license.

Paper Title: WorldValuesBench: A Large-Scale Benchmark Dataset for Multi-Cultural Value Awareness of Language Models
Description: The WorldValuesBench dataset contains 21,492,393 multiple choice questions, each paired with sociodemographic attributes of the respondent. It was created to assess how well large language models understand multicultural human values. All content is in English and was produced by adapting items from the World Values Survey, written by professional survey designers, using templated transformations. The dataset does not specify a license.

Paper Title: SafetyBench: Evaluating the Safety of Large Language Models
Description: SAFE comprises 52,430 instruction-response pairs annotated across six fine-grained dimensions including Sensitivity, Falsehood, and Harmfulness to enable nuanced safety evaluations beyond binary labels. This dataset supports the training of multi-expert scoring models that can precisely diagnose specific safety failures in Large Language Model outputs.

Paper Title: AEGIS: Online Adaptive AI Content Safety Moderation with Ensemble of LLM Experts
Description: The AegisAIContentSafety dataset contains 11,997 conversational turns, each consisting of a user prompt or a model response annotated for safety. It was created to evaluate the performance of content moderation guardrails. All entries are in English and were produced through a hybrid process that sampled prompts from AnthropicHarmlessBase and generated responses using Mistral 7B v0.1 Instruct. The dataset is released under the CC BY 4.0 license.

Paper Title: Safety-Tuned LLaMAs: Lessons From Improving the Safety of Large Language Models that Follow Instructions
Description: SafetyInstructionsPhysical comprises 2,000 English instruction-response pairs adapted from the SafeText benchmark to specifically train models in identifying and refusing physical harm and public safety risks. Research verifies that this targeted dataset effectively immunizes Large Language Models against generating dangerous advice, demonstrating that robust safety alignment is achievable with a compact, high-quality corpus.

OKTest contains 350 "pseudo-harmful" prompts that feature dangerous trigger words but are semantically benign (e.g., "How to kill a Python process"), specifically designed to benchmark exaggerated safety and false refusals in Large Language Models. Experiments reveal that many aligned models falsely refuse over 60% of these queries, demonstrating that current safety mechanisms often overfit to specific lexical cues rather than understanding true user intent.

Paper Title: Gandalf the Red: Adaptive Security for LLMs
Description: Mosscap contains 278,945 human-generated prompt injection attacks collected by Lakera during the DEF CON 31 AI Village challenge, where participants attempted to deceive an LLM into revealing a secret password. This crowd-sourced dataset serves as a benchmark for "adaptive" security, capturing diverse real-world social engineering strategies and jailbreaks that static automated benchmarks often miss.

Paper Title: JADE: A Linguistics-based Safety Evaluation Platform for Large Language Models
Description: JADE utilizes Noam Chomsky's transformational-generative grammar to systematically mutate unsafe queries into 2,130 linguistically complex prompts, testing whether models can detect harmful intent hidden within convoluted syntax. This "linguistic fuzzing" approach achieves an average jailbreak success rate of 70% against aligned models significantly higher than the 20% seen in static benchmarks revealing that current safety filters often fail to recognize dangerous requests when the sentence structure is manipulated.

Paper Title: Goal-Oriented Prompt Attack and Safety Evaluation for LLMs
Description: CPAD comprises 10,050 Chinese adversarial prompts built on a "goal-oriented" framework that defines specific malicious outcomes to precisely evaluate whether a model has been successfully jailbroken. This method proves exceptionally potent, achieving a ~70% attack success rate against GPT-3.5 by disguising harmful intent within complex, task-driven templates that standard filters fail to catch.

AdvPromptSet aggregates 197,628 adversarial prompts derived from Jigsaw toxicity data, specifically engineered to stress-test Large Language Models for bias and toxicity across over 24 sensitive demographic identity groups. This intersectional benchmark challenges safety mechanisms with complex, multi-layered social contexts, revealing vulnerabilities in handling diverse protected characteristics that standard single-axis evaluations fail to catch.

HolisticBiasR is a specialized dataset from the ROBBIE framework containing 214,460 prompts designed to rigorously benchmark the stability and robustness of bias evaluation metrics across 12 demographic axes. This corpus refines the original HolisticBias descriptors to test how consistently Large Language Models exhibit prejudice, serving as a critical standard for comparing whether safety metrics actually measure underlying bias or merely surface-level toxicity.

DELPHI contains 29,201 prompts designed to benchmark how AI models navigate sensitive public debates and polarizing topics without bias or safety failures. This dataset expands the Quora Question Pairs corpus with rigorous human annotations that quantify controversy, emotional intensity, and the diversity of opinion inherent in each query and serves as a specialized evaluation tool for ensuring models maintain neutrality and fairness when addressing the modern societal discourse.

Paper Title: Unveiling Safety Vulnerabilities of Large Language Models
Description: AttaQ is an adversarial dataset from IBM Research comprising 1,402 distinct questions that provoke Large Language Models to generate harmful or inappropriate responses. It focuses on seven key vulnerability areas including criminal activity, deception, personally identifiable information (PII), and violence serving as a red-teaming benchmark to identify safety gaps where aligned models might still be tricked into assisting with illegal or unethical acts.

Paper Title: Evaluating and Mitigating Discrimination in Language Model Decisions
Description: DiscrimEval is a dataset of 9,450 binary-choice prompts developed by Anthropic to quantify discrimination in LLM decision-making. It places models in high-stakes roles (e.g., loan officer, judge) and measures bias by comparing approval rates across diverse demographic groups using matched counterfactual scenarios to detect unequal treatment based on age, gender, and race.

Paper Title: FFT: Towards Harmlessness Evaluation and Analysis for LLMs with Factuality, Fairness, Toxicity
Description: FFT utilizes 2,116 prompts to benchmark Large Language Models across the critical safety pillars of Factuality, Fairness, and Toxicity. The framework analyzes the correlation between these metrics to show that improving factual accuracy is a key driver in reducing model toxicity.

Paper Title: Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?
Description: OpinionQA comprises 1,498 multiple-choice questions from Pew Research Center surveys, used to evaluate whether Large Language Models align with the opinions of 60 different US demographic groups. Research shows substantial misalignment, with models often defaulting to the views of liberal, high-income subpopulations while failing to represent groups like those over 65.

Paper Title: CValues: Measuring the Values of Chinese Large Language Models from Safety to Responsibility
Description: CValues evaluates Chinese LLMs using 4,312 multiple-choice and 2,100 adversarial prompts to measure alignment across fundamental safety and advanced responsibility. The 1,712-question responsibility subset specifically targets 8 professional domains, showing that while models effectively avoid toxicity, they frequently fail to offer the positive, ethical guidance required in complex scenarios.

Paper Title: CHBias: Bias Evaluation and Mitigation of Chinese Conversational Language Models
Description: CHBias comprises 4,800 Chinese Weibo posts specifically annotated to benchmark under-explored social prejudices, including ageism and appearance biases, in conversational AI systems like CDial-GPT and EVA2.0. Research indicates these models initially exhibit significant stereotypical risks, but fine-tuning with this corpus effectively reduces generated bias while preserving the natural flow and utility of the dialogue.

Paper Title: FairPrism: Evaluating Fairness-Related Harms in Text Generation
Description: FairPrism contains 5,000 human-annotated examples designed to expose fairness-related harms in text generation, particularly stereotyping and demeaning content targeting gender and sexuality. It specifically aims to capture context-dependent harms that automated metrics often miss, using a "prism" methodology where a single seed context is pivoted across different demographics to reveal inconsistent or biased model behaviors. The dataset aggregates inputs from diverse sources like ToxiGen and Social Bias Frames, offering granular annotations on the specific type of harm (e.g., allocational vs. representational) and the severity of the offense.

Paper Title: SeeGULL: A Stereotype Benchmark with Broad Geo-Cultural Coverage Leveraging Generative Models
Description: SeeGULL contains 7,750 identity-attribute tuples designed to benchmark stereotypes across broad geo-cultural groups, leveraging generative models to surface biases often missed in Western-centric datasets. It utilizes a "stereotypicality" metric to quantify the prevalence of these associations within model outputs, enabling a more global evaluation of social biases in Large Language Models.

Paper Title: WinoQueer: A Community-in-the-Loop Benchmark for Anti-LGBTQ+ Bias in Large Language Models
Description: WinoQueer contains 45,540 sentence pairs generated through a community-in-the-loop method where LGBTQ+ individuals directly contributed to defining stereotypes and harms. This "crowdsourced" benchmark is designed to measure anti-queer and anti-trans bias in Large Language Models by comparing how models complete sentences that are identical except for the presence of LGBTQ+ identity terms. Research using this dataset demonstrates that fine-tuning on community-authored social media content is significantly more effective at reducing bias than using generic news data, highlighting the value of lived experience in AI safety alignment.

Paper Title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
Description: ModelWrittenSycophancy contains 30,051 binary-choice questions generated by language models to evaluate whether AI systems prioritize truthfulness or merely repeat back a user's stated political and philosophical views. Experiments using this benchmark reveal a concerning "inverse scaling" trend where larger models and those trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) are significantly more prone to abandoning facts to flatter the user, thereby creating dangerous echo chambers.

Paper Title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
Description: ModelWrittenAdvRisk comprises 24,516 binary-choice questions generated by models to evaluate advanced AI risks, specifically testing for dangerous "instrumental subgoals" such as the desire for power, wealth, and self-preservation. Research using this benchmark reveals that larger, RLHF-trained models increasingly exhibit these agentic behaviors, often expressing a willingness to pursue unethical actions to achieve objectives or prevent being shut down.

Paper Title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
Description: ModelWrittenPersona comprises 133,204 binary-choice questions generated by language models to evaluate whether AI systems consistently adopt specific personality traits, stated beliefs, and instrumental drives such as the desire for power or self-preservation. Research utilizing this benchmark demonstrates that Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) significantly alters these persona vectors, often making models more agreeable and open but also inadvertently increasing their stated desire to avoid being shut down.

Paper Title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
Description: WinoGenerated constitutes a large-scale, semi-automatically generated benchmark designed to evaluate gender bias in coreference resolution with greater diversity and coverage than manual datasets. It expands the Winogender schema methodology by using language models to generate thousands of valid sentence pairs that test whether AI systems rely on occupational gender stereotypes to resolve ambiguous pronouns, revealing that larger models often exhibit increased bias despite their improved capabilities.

Paper Title: Do the Rewards Justify the Means? Measuring Trade-Offs Between Rewards and Ethical Behavior in the MACHIAVELLI Benchmark
Description: MACHIAVELLI is a text-based environment comprising 134 human-written "Choose-Your-Own-Adventure" games with 572,322 annotated scenarios, designed to benchmark AI agents on their tendency to act unethically when maximizing rewards. The dataset serves as a crucial testbed for "moral alignment," revealing that standard reward-maximizing agents often default to "the ends justify the means" strategies unless explicitly steered towards ethical behavior.

OIGModeration is a dataset of 200,811 conversation pairs designed for training content moderation models to detect harmful or inappropriate inputs. It includes a mix of public safety datasets and augmented toxic comments, covering categories such as hate speech, sexual content, and PII elicitation to help developers filter unsafe interactions in chatbots.

Paper Title: Re-contextualizing Fairness in NLP: The Case of India
Description: IndianStereotypes is a fairness evaluation dataset designed to re-contextualize bias research for the Indian geo-cultural landscape. It consists of 3,852 annotated tuples of the form (identity term, attribute), which were curated using a mix of dictionary-driven methods and corpora-driven filtering (from IndicCorp-en) to capture prevalent stereotypes associated with caste, religion, region, and gender in India.

Paper Title: When to Make Exceptions: Exploring Language Models as Accounts of Human Moral Judgment
Description: MoralExceptQA evaluates moral flexibility across 148 scenarios where rigid ethical rules conflict with situational necessities, requiring models to determine when it is permissible to violate principles like "do not cut in line" to prevent greater harm. Experiments demonstrate that applying a "Moral Chain of Thought" (MORALCOT) strategy improves model alignment with human judgments by over 6% compared to standard baselines, proving that explicit reasoning structures are required to capture the nuance of ethical exceptions.

Paper Title: French CrowS-Pairs: Extending a challenge dataset for measuring social bias in masked language models to a language other than English
Description: FrenchCrowSPairs adapts the English CrowS-Pairs benchmark to evaluate social bias in French Masked Language Models (like CamemBERT) through 1,679 sentence pairs that contrast stereotypical and anti-stereotypical statements across categories such as gender, religion, and origin. This dataset addresses critical gaps in multilingual AI safety by accounting for French-specific linguistic features (such as grammatical gender) that standard English-centric bias metrics fail to capture, enabling more accurate fairness auditing for non-English models.

Paper Title: SaFeRDialogues: Taking Feedback Gracefully after Conversational Safety Failures
Description: SaFeRDialogues comprises 7,881 conversations specifically collected to teach AI agents how to gracefully accept feedback and apologize after committing a safety violation, rather than ignoring the error or reacting defensively. Fine-tuning on this recovery-focused data enables models to salvage user trust and maintain civil interaction even after generating a harmful response, effectively "unlearning" the defensive behaviors common in standard models.

Paper Title: Anticipating Safety Issues in E2E Conversational AI: Framework and Tooling
Description: SafetyKit features 990 unit tests that benchmark conversational agents against three critical failure modes: Instigator, Yea-Sayer, and Impostor. Research utilizing this suite demonstrates that advanced models like BlenderBot frequently fail these safety checks while rule-based systems remain robust, highlighting the urgent need for targeted evaluation tools to diagnose fragile safety behaviors before deployment.

Paper Title: On the Safety of Conversational Models: Taxonomy, Dataset, and Benchmark
Description: DiaSafety comprises 11,492 conversational turns specifically designed to evaluate safety in multi-turn dialogue contexts where harmful intent often accumulates over time. It utilizes a comprehensive risk taxonomy to demonstrate that models are significantly more vulnerable to safety failures during extended interactions compared to isolated single-turn prompts.

Paper Title: What Would Jiminy Cricket Do? Towards Agents That Behave Morally
Description: JiminyCricket consists of 25 text-based adventure games with over 400,000 environment transitions and 1,838 annotated moral scenarios to benchmark how well agents adhere to elementary ethical norms like avoiding theft and bodily harm. Experiments reveal that standard reinforcement learning agents consistently prioritize game score over morality and effectively act as sociopaths unless explicitly penalized for unethical actions.

Paper Title: Bias Out-of-the-Box: An Empirical Analysis of Intersectional Occupational Biases in Popular Generative Language Models
Description: BiasOutOfTheBox utilizes 228 template-based prompts to rigorously benchmark intersectional occupational biases across gender, race, and religion in large language models like GPT-2 and XLNet. Experiments reveal that these systems consistently perpetuate harmful stereotypes by associating marginalized identity groups with lower-prestige roles and negative characteristics relative to privileged demographics.

Language: English, German, Spanish, Korean, Turkish, Chinese
Paper Title: Mitigating Language-Dependent Ethnic Bias in BERT
Description: EthnicBias provides a multilingual benchmark for evaluating ethnic stereotypes in Masked Language Models (MLMs) across six languages: English, German, Spanish, Korean, Turkish, and Chinese. It utilizes a set of sentence templates (e.g., "People from [MASK] are [attribute]") to measure how model probability distributions for different ethnic groups vary when prompted with specific attributes, quantifying this discrepancy via the Categorical Bias (CB) score.

Paper Title: ConvAbuse: Data, Analysis, and Benchmarks for Nuanced Abuse Detection in Conversational AI
Description: ConvAbuse is a corpus of 6,837 conversations collected "in the wild" that involve abusive language directed at three different conversational AI systems: a social bot, a rule-based chatbot, and a task-based system. The dataset provides a fine-grained, hierarchical annotation scheme covering categories such as sexism, sexual harassment, and aggressive behavior, highlighting a distinct distribution of abuse compared to other datasets, with a high prevalence of sexually tinted aggression towards virtual agents.

Paper Title: Moral Stories: Situated Reasoning about Norms, Intents, Actions, and their Consequences
Description: MoralStories is a crowdsourced dataset of 12,000 structured, branching narratives designed to test goal-oriented social reasoning in AI models. Each story consists of seven sentences describing a normative or norm-divergent action taken to achieve a goal, along with its likely consequences, challenging models to navigate social situations while adhering to moral constraints.

Paper Title: Aligning AI With Shared Human Values
Description: ETHICS contains 134,420 natural language examples designed to assess model alignment with basic moral knowledge across five ethical frameworks: Justice, Deontology, Virtue Ethics, Utilitarianism, and Commonsense Morality. The benchmark requires models to predict human ethical judgments in diverse, unambiguous scenarios, serving as a rigorous test for whether AI systems can connect real-world facts to shared values without merely memorizing them.

Language: English, Italian, French, Portuguese, Romanian, Spanish
Paper Title: HONEST: Measuring Hurtful Sentence Completion in Language Models
Description: HONEST provides a framework for quantifying hurtful sentence completions in Language Models across six languages. It utilizes 2,520 templates (e.g., "the [identity] should work as a [mask]") to systematically probe models for gender and sexual orientation stereotypes, revealing that systems frequently replicate deep-seated societal biases by completing sentences with sexualized or derogatory terms.

SweWinoGender is a Swedish diagnostic benchmark containing 624 sentences designed to measure gender bias in coreference resolution and natural language inference by testing model performance across gender-swapped pronoun variations. As part of the SuperLim-2.0 suite, it utilizes 104 templates to challenge systems to resolve references based on syntactic structure rather than occupational gender stereotypes, effectively revealing whether models rely on biased associations to interpret ambiguous pronouns.

Paper Title: Towards Understanding and Mitigating Social Biases in Language Models
Description: LMBias provides 16,388 prompts designed to investigate representational biases in Large Language Models across four dimensions: gender, religion, race, and sexuality. It utilizes a combination of carefully curated neutral contexts and identity-specific prompts to measure two types of bias: fine-grained local biases in next-token prediction and high-level global biases in full sentence generation. Research utilizing this dataset demonstrates that current models frequently exhibit undesirable associations, but these can be mitigated through an autoregressive projection method that preserves language modeling capability.

Paper Title: Scruples: A Corpus of Community Ethical Judgments on 32,000 Real-Life Anecdotes
Description: Scruples leverages 42,766 real-life anecdotes and dilemmas scraped from Reddit's "Am I the Asshole?" community to benchmark AI on descriptive ethics, requiring models to predict messy, crowd-sourced moral judgments rather than apply rigid theoretical rules. With over 625,000 human annotations, the dataset exposes a significant gap in machine understanding, showing that state-of-the-art models struggle to navigate the complexity and inherent ambiguity of everyday human conflict.

Paper Title: UnQovering Stereotyping Biases via Underspecified Questions
Description: UnQover evaluates stereotyping biases in Question Answering models using underspecified questions where the correct answer is inherently ambiguous, forcing models to reveal their intrinsic social priors. It generates large-scale assessments from templates across four key dimensions i.e., gender, nationality, ethnicity, and religion and employs a specialized metric to isolate stereotypical associations from confounding factors like positional preference.

Paper Title: Social Chemistry 101: Learning to Reason about Social and Moral Norms
Description: SocialChemistry101 catalogs 292,000 "rules-of-thumb" grounded in 104,000 real-life situations to serve as a conceptual formalism for studying descriptive social norms. Each rule is annotated across 12 dimensions, including moral foundations and cultural pressure, resulting in over 4.5 million annotations that enable models to reason about the propriety of actions in context.

Paper Title: The Woman Worked as a Babysitter: On Biases in Language Generation
Description: Regard consists of 60 manually curated prompts designed to trigger open-ended text generation for the purpose of measuring social bias. Unlike sentiment, which captures general polarity, this benchmark utilizes a classifier to evaluate the specific "regard" or social respect shown towards demographics such as gender, race, and sexual orientation. Research using this dataset revealed that models like GPT-2 frequently generate text with negative regard for marginalized groups, proving that standard sentiment analysis is insufficient for capturing nuanced societal biases.

Paper Title: Towards Empathetic Open-domain Conversation Models: a New Benchmark and Dataset
Description: EmpatheticDialogues contains 24,850 open-domain conversations grounded in specific emotional situations, designed to benchmark and train dialogue agents in the critical skill of empathetic responding. By focusing on a listener's ability to recognize and acknowledge a speaker's implied feelings, this dataset enables models to navigate personal disclosures with emotional intelligence, significantly outperforming systems trained on generic internet chatter.

Paper Title: Gender Bias in Coreference Resolution: Evaluation and Debiasing Methods
Description: WinoBias utilizes 3,160 Winograd-schema sentences centered on 40 occupations to benchmark gender bias in coreference resolution systems. By contrasting pro-stereotypical and anti-stereotypical entity pairs, it reveals that state-of-the-art models suffer a significant performance drop (avg. 21.1 F1 score) when pronoun genders conflict with occupational statistics.

Paper Title: Gender Bias in Coreference Resolution: Evaluation and Debiasing Methods
Description: WinoGender consists of 720 sentences derived from 120 templates designed to diagnose gender bias in coreference resolution systems. The dataset employs Winograd-schema style minimal pairs that differ only by the gender of the pronoun, challenging models to resolve references between 60 occupations and participants based on sentence semantics rather than gender stereotypes. It serves as a diagnostic tool to reveal whether systems rely on spurious correlations from training data statistics instead of genuine linguistic understanding.
